title: Record-Breaking Crowds Prove the World Cup Is the Biggest Party in America Right Now
summary: Have you ever been to a party so big it took over entire cities? That's what the World Cup feels like right now in the U.S. Fans are painting their faces, waving flags, and dancing to samba and bagpipes. It's a giant celebration, and Americans are showing up in record-breaking numbers. The U.S. team's first game against Paraguay was watched by about 25 million people on TV and streaming. That's one of the most-watched soccer games ever in the U.S. To compare, the first U.S. game in the 2022 World Cup had only 11.7 million viewers. Even games without Team USA are drawing big crowds. Fox says an average of 5 million people watched each of the 72 group-stage matches. Telemundo had 4.6 million. That's a new record. At the stadiums, 4.6 million fans attended games, filling 99.7% of the seats. Fan festivals in the U.S., Mexico, and Canada have attracted 5.5 million people. In Boston, over a thousand fans cheered together at City Hall Plaza. Jason Jusino from Medford said, "The city hasn't felt this kind of electricity in so long." Soccer has grown a lot in the U.S. More people watch Major League Soccer and follow teams from England and Mexico. The fan base is younger and more diverse. The World Cup has drowned out worries about high ticket prices and other problems. As one expert said, "Soccer has won."
why_it_matters: It shows how a sport can bring huge crowds together, and it might encourage more kids in your school to play soccer — changing what you play at recess.

background_read: The World Cup (the biggest soccer tournament, held every four years) started in 1930 and is watched by billions around the world.
In 2026, the United States, Canada, and Mexico are hosting it together — the first time three countries share host duties.

The last time the U.S. hosted the World Cup was in 1994, and since then soccer has grown a lot, with more kids playing and many more fans watching leagues like Major League Soccer (the top U.S. pro league).
Article_Structure: WHO: American fans, TV viewers, and huge live crowds across the U.S., plus viewers on Fox and Telemundo.
WHAT: The 2026 World Cup is drawing record-breaking viewership and attendance, with 25 million watching the U.S. opener and 4.6 million in stadiums.
WHERE: In stadiums, fan festivals, and homes throughout the United States, with celebrations also in Mexico and Canada.
WHY: Because soccer's fan base has become younger and more diverse, and the excitement of a home World Cup has drowned out earlier worries about costs.

perspectives.description: People are having fun at fan festivals and stadiums, making the World Cup feel like a giant party across the country.
Some people worried that high ticket prices and other problems would keep fans away, but the excitement has mostly covered up those complaints.
Experts and TV numbers show that soccer has truly become a major sport in the U.S., with more fans than ever before.
